name: Jade Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and run the die cutter that stamps rubber gaskets for pumps. I have a vocational certificate and have worked these machines long enough to know when a sheet is feeding crooked. I set the guard, check the first gaskets and call maintenance if the blade drags. I like a stack whose edges match without trimming.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life at home like, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner keeps the books for a local shop, and our grown children have their own flats. We rent and have about four months of expenses saved. My pay is typical for this machine job, and some similar factories are within a reasonable journey. I use AI now and then for a recipe or a short explanation, once I can check it. I'd like to stop at 67 in 2035 if documented income after work covers rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the cutter crew that a quieter AI story leaves us making the same gaskets. A program might count orders faster, but a bent blade still makes a bad edge. We should keep the first-sheet check on the paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our four-month reserve and my partner's regular shop pay make the current bills manageable. I do not assume a machine can never break, but several factories could use an experienced cutter. This gives us time to make retirement sums rather than rush them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep checking the first ten gaskets after each rubber-sheet change and record blade drag for maintenance. My partner and I will add a small amount from each new wage payment to the reserve after rent. We will list the costs that would remain if I stopped work at 67.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about work and income in this picture. A smooth gasket edge is easier to judge than a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you spot a dragging blade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A dragging blade leaves a rough lip that catches my glove. I stop the cutter and show maintenance the first rejected gasket before the rest of the sheet goes through. I do not put my hand under the blade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the four-month reserve cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months saved can handle a short repair, but it cannot replace a wage forever. My partner's shop hours are regular at present. The list of rent and food will tell us what the reserve needs to sit beside.

say: **First-sheet checks** still matter on the gasket cutter.
The plant should keep **paid quality time** rather than assume faster counting is enough.
think: Our **four-month reserve** and partner wage cover current bills.
Some nearby factories offer options if the **die cutter** has a long stoppage.
do: **Keep** checking gaskets and logging blade drag for maintenance.
**Save** new wage money after rent and list costs before any retirement decision.
feel: **Calm** about present work and household income.
S0.quote: A smooth gasket edge is easier to judge than a forecast.
fieldNote: Her **vocational skill** and typical pay sit alongside four months saved and some nearby factory options.
The **new reserve deposits** come from wages; the cost list is preparation, not a promise of retirement income.

steps.text: Keep checking first ten gaskets and logging blade drag
Save new cutter wages after monthly rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software may choose cutting layouts before robots run the press. I would try a layout screen after another operator proves it saves rubber, but I want a paid lesson and the guard checked. We should compare the promised savings with actual shift hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A better layout could mean fewer setup hours for me. Four months saved helps, though a regular mortgage or rent does not shrink with a rota. My occasional AI use at home does not teach me a factory screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll compare the posted setup rota with four recent pay slips. If the supervisor approves a tested AI-assisted layout screen, I'll learn its controls with the lead operator on a paid shift and compare its first cut with a measured paper pattern. If a funded paid guarded die-maintenance course is offered, I'll enrol and practise on a stopped cutter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible paid-hour cut, but interested in a layout that really works. Rubber saved on a cutting layout does not pay a missing setup hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you verify a layout screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would measure the first gasket against the approved paper pattern and check where the screen puts its cuts. The lead must show me how to stop the layout before a bad sheet is stamped. I would not turn a suggested pattern into a live cut without the guard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove lost setup hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The setup line on the posted rota tells me what I am paid for. I would compare it with four pay slips and ask the supervisor about a real difference. A sales demonstration is not an hour on my payslip.

say: **Layout AI** may affect setup work before robots run the cutter.
Any new screen needs **paid guarded practice** and measured gaskets.
think: Fewer **paid setup hours** could reduce my own wage as cutting layouts improve.
My occasional **home AI use** is not the same skill as operating an approved factory layout screen.
do: **Compare** posted setup hours with pay slips.
**Learn** an approved tested layout with the lead on paid time and enrol in funded guarded maintenance if offered.
feel: **Anxious** about possible paid-hour loss despite interest in the screen.
S1.quote: Rubber saved on a cutting layout does not pay a missing setup hour.
fieldNote: Her **steady adaptability** waits for another operator to prove the layout, then accepts paid supervised use.
The **maintenance course** is distinct from the AI screen and needs an offered funded paid guarded practical place.

steps.text: Compare posted cutter setup rota with four pay slips
Learn approved tested AI layout with lead on paid shift
Enrol in die maintenance if funded paid guarded place offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI could plan the cuts by 2028, and robots might feed and stamp gaskets around 2031 when I am 63. That would be four years before I hope to stop. I want a written plan for the operator shifts, not a guess from a sales display.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the factory may cut a substantial part of the cutter rota if robots can make the whole gasket. Four months saved and some nearby factories give me time to look, but my partner's shop wage would not cover everything. I would not call 63 a retirement date without income figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for written staffing hours and a funded paid guarded place in gasket inspection. If it is offered, I'll enrol and take the practical check. If my cutter hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local packing roles only when net pay after travel covers our bills; once qualified, I'll also apply to posted gasket-inspection roles on the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because a large cut is possible but I have a few options. A real factory posting can help us; a factory rumour cannot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would gasket-inspection training test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainer should give me a gasket with a split rim and have me measure it and stop the guarded press. I need paid practice and covered fees. I will not claim to be an inspector after reading a leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What terms make another job workable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look for the posted base wage, paid hours and site. The bus cost comes off before I compare the new job with rent and food. An inspection job also needs a practical pass, not just my current operator experience.

say: **2031 robots** may run gasket presses when I am 63.
We need **written operator hours** before a new line changes the rota.
think: A substantial **cutter-hour loss** could come before retirement is affordable.
Our **four-month reserve** and some local jobs give time, not permanent income.
do: **Request** written hours and attend funded paid guarded inspection if offered.
**Apply** to posted safe local packing or qualified inspection if hours fall and net pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about substantial possible wage loss, with some local alternatives.
S2.quote: A real factory posting can help us; a factory rumour cannot.
fieldNote: She expects a **possible substantial cut**, yet four months saved and several nearby plants give her choices.
The **inspection application** follows offered funded paid guarded teaching and qualification; both paths need posted safe local work at viable net pay.

steps.text: Enrol in gasket inspection if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply to posted safe local packing if hours fall and net pay covers bills
Apply to posted safe local inspection if qualified, hours fall, net pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI may plan cutting in 2031 and capable robots could handle the press about 2034, when I am 66. That is close to my hoped-for stop at 67. It would be foolish to call the machine a threat or a blessing before we know the household income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The four-month reserve would give us some room if shifts fell, but not an extra year of pay. If documented income covers our bills at 67, I can stop in 2035. If it does not, I need a safe paid job for longer, whether here or at another plant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I will request written post-work income figures and set them beside rent and food. If they cover the bills, I'll stop the cutter shift at 67 in 2035. If I am still working when robot presses arrive in 2034 and my hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local cutter roles only if net pay after travel covers our costs; I'll take funded paid guarded inspection training if an offered place is required for a real posted inspection job, then apply after qualifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious until we know the figures, because the press may change in the year before my planned stop. The four-month reserve is a pause button, not a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which figures decide whether 2035 works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need income that would actually arrive after my wages stop, plus rent and food on the same page. We will not assume an age brings a payment. If the balance fails, I keep looking for safe paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a new cutter role need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cutter posting needs a guarded machine, real paid hours and a base wage that works after the bus fare. A posted inspection role needs the funded paid practical pass too. I would not leave this shift for an advert without a real offer.

say: **2031 cutting AI** comes before press robots around 2034.
I would stop at **67** only if documented income covers costs.
think: Our **four-month reserve** cannot replace a year of cutter pay.
If the figures fail, I need **safe paid work** after 2035.
do: **Compare** written post-work income and stop cutter work at 67 only if bills are covered.
**Apply** to safe posted local cutter or qualified inspection work if still employed, hours fall and net pay works.
feel: **Anxious** until retirement affordability and future hours are clear.
S3.quote: The four-month reserve is a pause button, not a wage.
fieldNote: Her **2035 stop** is a real conditional exit based on documented household income, not an age entitlement.
If still employed, a **cutter application** needs a posted safe local role and viable net pay; inspection adds funded paid guarded qualification.

steps.text: Stop cutter shift at 67 in 2035 if documented income covers bills
Attend inspection if funded paid guarded place offered for posted job
Apply to posted safe local cutter if employed in 2034, hours fall, net pay sufficient
Apply to posted safe local inspection if qualified, employed in 2034, hours fall, net pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could plan cuts in 2036 when I am 68, and robots might run the die press around 2039 when I am 71. If our numbers work, I will have stopped in 2035. If they do not, a longer warning gives me time to find real paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months saved and my partner's steady shop income help, but neither proves we can stop at 67. I want the actual income after work beside our bills. If it falls short, I might still be on a factory rota after 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I will compare documented post-work income with rent, food and other costs this year. I'll keep the paid cutter shift while we check. If the figures cover bills, I'll stop in 2035 at 67; if I am still employed after 2036 and hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local manufacturing jobs only where net pay after travel covers us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy until the income is verified, but ten years leaves room to check. A paper retirement date cannot run the gasket press for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make 2035 affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need the actual monthly amount available after my wage ends, not a guess at a benefit. The shop income belongs in the sum at the hours my partner really works. If we cannot cover rent and food, I stay on a safe paid rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would a later application happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the posted base wage, shift hours, guard rules and travel cost. I would send an application only if I was still working and the cutter hours were down after 2036. If I have stopped with enough income, I will not search for a new press.

say: **2036 planning AI** and later press robots leave time to check income.
I will **stop in 2035** only when household costs are covered.
think: Four months saved is **not retirement income**.
If post-work income falls short, I may still be **working after 2036**.
do: **Check** documented post-work income against bills and stop at 67 only if affordable.
**Keep** earning meanwhile; apply later only if still employed, hours fall and safe local net pay suffices.
feel: **Uneasy** about unverified future income, with time to plan.
S4.quote: A paper retirement date cannot run the gasket press for me.
fieldNote: The **2035 exit** depends on documented post-work income and is not an assumed benefit or automatic age rule.
The **post-2036 search** requires continued employment, lost hours and an actual safe local manufacturing post at adequate net pay.

steps.text: Compare documented post-work income with rent and food
Keep working paid gasket-cutter shifts while checking figures
Stop cutter shift at 67 in 2035 if documented income covers bills
Apply to posted safe local gasket work if employed after 2036, hours fall, net pay sufficient

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most. If robots run the cutter by 2031, I could lose hours at 63 before we know whether 67 is affordable. Written shifts, a funded paid guarded inspection place and actual safe local jobs with enough pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the first gasket from a new rubber sheet. A neat circle can still have a split edge that fails inside a pump.

headlineQuote: A neat circle can still have a split edge that fails inside a pump.
portrait: **Jade**, 58, is an experienced gasket die-cutter operator with a vocational certificate and occasional checked AI use.
She and her shop-bookkeeper partner have **grown children**, typical operator pay, four months saved and some nearby factories.
Her **centrist outlook** asks for measured results; she accepts a proven layout screen only with approved paid guarded practice.
She is **anxious** about fast lost cutter hours; stopping at 67 depends on documented income covering rent and food.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring gasket-press robots around 2031, cutting hours at 63.
whatWouldHelp: **Written shifts**, funded paid guarded inspection and real safe local work with viable net pay would help.
